article.title: How to Fix a Door That Sticks or Rubs
article.summary: Fix a sticking door without taking it off: find where it rubs, tighten and lengthen hinge screws, repair stripped holes, and only plane as a last resort.
article.body:
Most sticking doors aren't warped, they're sagging on loose hinges. This guide shows you how to pull the door back into line, step by step, before you ever reach for a plane.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Steps

  1. Find where it rubs

    Close the door slowly and watch the gap around it. Look for shiny, worn paint on the door edge or frame, or slide a sheet of paper around the closed door to find tight spots. A door that rubs at the top on the latch side is usually sagging from the top hinge.

    Done right: you've marked exactly where the door rubs with a light pencil line.

  2. Tighten every hinge screw

    Open the door and tighten all the screws in each hinge, on both the door and the frame. Test the door.

    Done right: no screw turns any further, and you've tested the door again.

  3. Drive a long screw into the top hinge

    Remove one of the short screws from the top hinge on the frame side, ideally the one closest to the doorstop, and replace it with a 3-inch wood screw. It reaches the wall framing and pulls the hinge, and the door, up and back toward the frame.

    Done right: the gap at the top of the latch side has opened up and the door closes without rubbing.

  4. Repair stripped screw holes

    If a screw just spins, remove it, fill the hole with wood glue and a few wooden toothpicks or a golf tee, let the glue set, and trim the wood flush with a utility knife. Drive the screw back in.

    Done right: every hinge screw tightens firmly and holds.

  5. Sand or plane only what's left

    If the door still rubs, and especially if it only sticks in humid weather, sand or plane just the marked spot, a little at a time, testing often. For the top or bottom edge, take the door off its hinges first.

    Done right: the door closes and latches smoothly with an even gap around it.

  6. Seal any bare wood

    Prime and paint, or seal, any edge you sanded or planed. Bare wood soaks up moisture, swells, and the door will stick again.

    Done right: no bare wood is showing on any edge of the door.

Get it checked if: several doors start sticking at once, or you see new diagonal cracks in the drywall above door frames. That can mean the house is settling, which a contractor or structural engineer should look at.

FAQ

Why does my door stick in summer but not in winter?

Wood absorbs moisture in humid weather and swells. Sealing every edge of the door, including the top and bottom, reduces seasonal sticking.

How do I fix a door that won't latch?

First tighten the hinges and add a long screw to the top hinge. If the latch still misses, file the strike plate opening slightly or move the strike plate.

Can I plane a door without taking it off?

You can lightly sand or plane the latch-side edge in place. Take the door off its hinges to work on the top or bottom edge.
